articles.summary: Former England fast bowler James Anderson considering a future outside of playing cricket after Lancashire opt not to renew his contract; Anderson says decision made him question whether there was something "fundamentally wrong" with him as a person
articles.body:
Anderson - who first played List A cricket with Lancashire as a 17-year-old in 2000 - will see his 26-year association with the club end, despite taking 50 wickets at an average of 17 amid their struggles in Division Two of the County Championship in 2026.

Speaking on the BBC's Tailenders podcast, England's all-time leading wicket taker said the decision made him question whether something was "wrong" with his character after his side finished second bottom of the table.

"All of the way through the season myself and the head coach were like 'is it something we are doing? Could we be doing more to help the team?'" Anderson said.

"I finished the season thinking 'was it something I did? Was I doing something wrong?' - and then I get this news - now I am thinking that even more.

"I'm thinking 'this is happening again - is there something fundamentally wrong with me as a person?' Your head just races.

"I wanted to see my career out with Lancs. I don't know if my career is done, we will have to wait and see, but it would be nice at some point if someone would let me retire."

On the meeting with Lancashire, Anderson said: "I went in for what I thought was a conversation about how the team moves forward. It wasn't a great year for the team. Being captain I thought it was a chat about that.

"A couple of minutes in I realised it wasn't a conversation. I was being told they thought the best way for the team to move forward was without me. I was quite shocked. It was quite brief."

Despite the controversy surrounding the end of his Lancashire tenure, the seamer remains optimistic about a future within or outside of cricket.

He added: "I'm starting to get excited about the future, whether it's something different or playing cricket again. It's exciting.

"There are exciting challenges ahead. I have to attack it like that and not dwell too much on how or why it finished at Lancs.

"I am sad the way it ended with the club I supported as a kid but now I have thought about it I am quite excited for the future.

"I am always going to support Lancashire."

articles.summary: Christian Barmore was diagnosed with blood clots in his lungs in 2024. Two years later, he says a new diet and gym routine have him feeling better than ever.
articles.body:
FOXBOROUGH – Life changed for Christian Barmore .

Coming off a breakout 2023 season, the Patriots defensive tackle was diagnosed with blood clots in his lungs. This happened three months after the team gave him a four-year contract extension worth up to $92 million.

In 2024, he returned to play four games only to have recurring symptoms. The tough year force Barmore to make drastic changes. Two years later, the 27-year-old says his new lifestyle has him finally feeling like his old self.

Through six games this season, Barmore has three sacks and it's the most he's had since his pre-blood clot diagnosis.

"I feel like I'm back to my normal self," Barmore said. "I don't like talking about that blood clot (expletive) because ain't nobody expect that (expletive) to happen. But, I'm back to myself. I feel better than ever, you know what I'm saying? I feel like I'm just moving better, my weight's been better, my mobility been better. So it's just like every day I get better at everything I do. I feel better than I was last year for sure."

A second-round pick in 2021, Barmore looked like a future Pro Bowler in 2023. That season, he finished with a career-high 8.5 sacks, 16 quarterback hits and 13 tackles for loss. That led the organization to giving him a sizeable contract extension.

Following the diagnosis, Barmore's production waned. He made one sack in 2024 where he played in four games. Last season, the defensive tackle was limited almost every week. This was part of the Patriots' plan for him as he adjusted to being on blood thinners. Barmore played in all 17 games, but finished with 2 sacks and 11 quarterback hits.

Last year, Barmore started implementing new changes. The defensive tackle focused on his weight, nutrition and mobility. Barmore's diet consists of protein, carbs and vegetables. Although he admits he still hates broccoli, his body feels better.

He's also dedicated himself to the gym. Although the blood clot diagnosis was a nightmare, the new changes have been good for him.

"Yeah, man, it helps out," Barmore said. "I just be in the gym consistency and especially on off days and days, you don't want to. Especially if your body' sore. If you got a routine, that's what you do, especially if you don't want to do it. The days you don't want to do it, you gotta do it. I feel like that's a big part of your career, taking care of your body and making yourself feel good."

After making just 2 sacks last season, Barmore gas been more productive to start his season. He has 2 sacks in the last two games and his 3 total sacks are the most he's had since his career-year in 2023.

Barmore said he appreciates the Patriots new gym inside the brand-new New Balance Athletics Center. When he's in there, he likes to stare out the large windows at the team's practice field.

Of course, the new weight room isn't why he's in there in the first place.

"I don't care. New. Old. It could be in Alaska, as long as it's got a gym, I love it," Barmore said. "I feel good. I feel real good."

articles.title: 'Important to retrospect': Shreyas Iyer after India's 87-run defeat vs New Zealand in 4th T20I
articles.summary: India captain Shreyas Iyer admitted that his team's bowling let them down in the fourth T20I against New Zealand.
articles.body: India captain Shreyas Iyer admitted that his team's bowling let them down in the fourth T20I against New Zealand. After an 87-run defeat in Auckland on Friday, Iyer said the team needed to review its performance and find ways to bounce back in the final match.New Zealand posted a massive 259 for 7 after being asked to bat. Glenn Phillips led the charge with 107 off 49 balls, while Michael Bracewell smashed 65 off just 25 deliveries.Phillips took 32 runs off Nitish Kumar Reddy's 16th over, hitting four sixes in a row. Phillips and Bracewell combined to hit 16 sixes, while New Zealand struck 20 maximums in total.Iyer admits India's bowling fell shortSpeaking after the match, Iyer said India failed to control New Zealand's scoring, especially in the powerplay. He also praised Phillips for his outstanding batting display."We fell short in our bowling. The power play, especially in the third over, they got the momentum thereon. Exceptional shots from Glenn, some phenomenal shots, pure bliss. Important to retrospect, we have to see how to bounce back. I feel we can go back to the drawing board and execute," Iyer said at the post-match presentation ceremony.The Indian captain also spoke about the challenges of playing at Eden Park, which is known for its small boundaries and unusual dimensions. He said it can take time for players to adjust to the ground."We knew the dimensions were going to be like this. First time for some of them. Not easy to adapt. The way they executed in the first three games was magnificent. Great learning curve."Santner happy with New Zealand's bowling effortNew Zealand captain Mitchell Santner was pleased with the way his bowlers performed, particularly during the powerplay. He said the team managed to take important wickets and make good use of the conditions."With the wind, it didn't dew up. You have to bowl well against these guys and we did. We saw a couple fly through at the start. The guys bashed through and we managed to take wickets in the powerplay. There is a little on the wicket, which is what we want. On a wicket that bounces, it is quite good," Santner said.Santner also praised Bracewell for his quick-fire innings, which helped New Zealand push their total close to 260."The way he came in, from ball one to keep going to push the score to 260... nice to see Beasty get runs, he's striking well in the nets. We made some tough options of hitting down the ground against those lengths. Duff nailing hard lengths and getting two to start is nice."Phillips enjoys batting on Eden Park pitchPhillips, who scored his third T20I century, said the pitch offered good conditions for batting. He was happy to contribute to New Zealand's victory."It was fabulous. A really good pitch to bat on. We made the most of it. Nice to get a few runs and contribute (to the winning cause).You make the purple patch last," he said about his consistent show in the ongoing series.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'I want to build fielding as an attacking weapon': New Mumbai Indians fielding coach T Dilip
articles.summary: Newly appointed Mumbai Indians fielding coach T Dilip wants to make fielding one of the team's biggest strengths.
articles.body: Newly appointed Mumbai Indians fielding coach T Dilip wants to make fielding one of the team's biggest strengths. He believes that a strong fielding unit can change the course of a match and wants to build a culture based on trust, respect and enjoyment.Dilip, who has previously worked as India's fielding coach, was one of three new members of the Mumbai Indians support staff announced on Friday.Speaking in a video shared by the franchise, Dilip said wearing the Mumbai Indians badge came with both pride and responsibility."Mumbai badge is a privilege and as well as a responsibility. As a Mumbai Indians team, I want to build fielding as an attacking weapon in the field," he said.Focus on the small thingsDilip believes fielding is not just about taking spectacular catches or producing brilliant run-outs. He wants players to understand that even small efforts on the field can make a big difference to the result of a match."We generally see catches, we generally see run-outs. Once players recognise that it's not the spectacular highlights which is highlighted, but the 1% factors which can impact a game, then automatically they will put in those efforts."And for us is to make sure that in a practice or a match, we create that environment where players having fun on the field, enjoy the field, and go out there. Sometimes you may have a bad day in your primary skills, whether a batting or bowling, but still you can impact a game through fielding."He also stressed the importance of building trust among players. According to Dilip, it takes time and depends on how teammates connect with each other both on and off the field."I think it's built over a period, because it's not only just what happens on the field, but I think how we interact and spend time with each other off the field, because it gives you an insight about what that person thinks."'Trust helps you enter the dressing room'Dilip has worked with several Mumbai Indians players during his time with the Indian team. He said his previous association with them would help him settle into the dressing room, but he knows that building trust within a new setup requires consistent effort."I have worked with Rohit as a captain when I started, then Surya as a captain, Jasprit Bumrah, Tilak Varma, Naman Dhir, you name anyone, Deepak Chahar, Shardul Thakur. So acquaintance is always there, that really helps."But trust me, acquaintance helps you to come into the dressing room, but to earn that place in the dressing room, I think it's an everyday work - hard work, what we do and relationship and how can I help the team to take forward, whether it's through culture or work. That is where I want to earn that back again."Wants fielding efforts to be recognisedDilip also spoke about the fielding medal initiative at Mumbai Indians and praised the players for making it popular. However, he said he would first understand the team's existing culture and the head coach's approach before bringing in any new ideas."I think when it comes to fielding medal, you know, I am very, very happy that a great initiative was taken, and actually, it's the players who made it really big, the way they have taken it."But I feel end of the day, I am new to this Mumbai Indians setup, and as we know that there are certain traditions which already goes, and my way of working generally is whoever is the head coach is to understand their philosophy."I'll definitely have a chat with them and see what best can be introduced or in an existing environment what can be done. But definitely fielding is something I would like to be rewarded and recognised."Dilip wants to bring smiles back to MI fansThe new fielding coach also spoke about the support Mumbai Indians receive at the Wankhede Stadium. He believes the home crowd gives the players extra confidence, especially during difficult moments."When it comes to Wankhede, I have seen personally there's always tremendous support because it is small ground, it resonates, it feels like in a tougher situation there is someone else backing you all the time."I know at times, the results have not gone in favour where they are quite happy because expectations of Mumbai Indians were high, but I'm sure with their support and with the calibre and effort we try to put and we make sure that we bring back the smiles on their face, and we bring up a show where they'll always be entertained."Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'I want teams to fear Mumbai Indians even when we play away': New MI batting coach Robin Uthappa
articles.summary: Mumbai Indians batting coach Robin Uthappa wants the team to become a force not just at the Wankhede Stadium but also at every other venue in the IPL.
articles.body: Mumbai Indians batting coach Robin Uthappa wants the team to become a force not just at the Wankhede Stadium but also at every other venue in the IPL. He believes the five-time champions must win back the trust of their fans after a disappointing 2025 season.Mumbai Indians finished ninth among 10 teams in IPL 2025. Uthappa knows the team, under head coach Kieron Pollard, has a lot of work to do to return to its winning ways.Speaking to the franchise's website, Uthappa said Mumbai Indians would once again begin their journey as underdogs and would have to earn the support of their fans.“Today, we find ourselves back in that similar situation right now where the trust of the fans need to be earned again. We come in again as underdogs. it's been one full cycle, and we're back to where we started again, which is nice," Uthappa said.Uthappa wants MI to dominate away from homeUthappa believes Mumbai Indians have built a strong reputation at the Wankhede Stadium. However, he wants the team to carry the same confidence and fighting spirit to away venues.“We’re a force to reckon with at home. I want to take that same emotion, that same energy to every venue away from home. My goal would be to make sure that that sense of intimidation that teams feel when they come to Mumbai Indians, to the Paltan -- I want them to feel that same intimidation when we go away from home as well."And to be able to be on the same side of the Mumbai Indians fans. On the same side of the Paltan. So I’m looking forward to playing a part in that journey of earning the fans’ trust back and making sure that this underdog journey will be one to be remembered.”Wants to build confidence among domestic playersUthappa also spoke about his plans to work closely with domestic cricketers. He believes young players need clear guidance and support to understand their roles and improve their game."I would love to empower domestic cricketers and help them get clarity. That’s one of the most important aspects that the young cricketers need at this point in time, clarity of what they want to do, how they want to do it, and what is the process by which they’re going to achieve those aspects.“You’re also emotionally investing in their own journey, and then you’re rooting for them. You want them to do well. And so when they do well, it feels like personal achievement."He recalled how one of the players he had mentored earned a place in India's Test team. Uthappa said the achievement made him feel as if he had been selected himself."I remember when one of the lads I was working with and mentoring got picked up in the Indian Test squad, it felt like I got selected. It felt that emotional."That’s something that I’m looking forward to, especially with domestic cricketers. And communication is a big part of it, and those are conversations I’m genuinely looking forward to."'It just feels like destiny': Uthappa on MI returnUthappa described his appointment as Mumbai Indians batting coach as a special moment. He began his IPL career with the franchise in 2008 and is now starting his coaching journey in the league with the same team.In the inaugural IPL season, Uthappa scored 320 runs in 14 matches for Mumbai Indians at an average of 35.55 and a strike rate of 114.69.Speaking in a video shared by the franchise on social media, he expressed his happiness at returning to MI."I am just genuinely happy to be back ... thrilled about this and delighted to have this opportunity to work with this special set of cricketers and this franchise," Uthappa said."Incredible, and it just feels like destiny, to be honest. As in, I started my IPL career with Mumbai Indians and I start my IPL coaching career with Mumbai Indians, which seems like destiny to me."Uthappa recalls playing alongside Sachin TendulkarUthappa, who represented India in 46 ODIs and 13 T20Is between 2005 and 2015, also looked back at his first IPL season. He remembered the excitement of being picked by Mumbai Indians in the 2008 auction and getting the opportunity to share the dressing room with his idol Sachin Tendulkar.At the time, Uthappa was in Australia with the Indian team for the CB Series when the IPL auction took place."So back in 2008, when I got into the franchise, I remember we were in Australia, playing the CB Series in Australia when the auctions happened, and I knew that I was going to be playing with my hero, Sachin Paaji over here."So for me, that was really exciting feeling, because everyone was finding their feet in that first season, and including the franchises and players and teams, and the IPL itself. We had, I would say, a fairly decent season, could have been better.“We had injuries, and Paaji (Sachin Tendulkar) missed a big part of that tournament, and then Bhajjupa (Harbhajan Singh) captained as well, and Sanath (Sanath Jayasuriya) played really well, Polly (Shaun Pollock) played really well."Uthappa went on to represent six franchises in the IPL. He won the title with Kolkata Knight Riders in 2014 and Chennai Super Kings in 2021. He finished his IPL career with 4,952 runs from 205 matches.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Ireland Cricket: Jai Moondra takes six wickets as Ireland level series against Namibia
articles.summary: Seamer Jai Moondra finishes with the best ever figures for an Ireland bowler in one-day international cricket as the tourists level their five-game series against Namibia with a comprehensive 130-run victory.
articles.body:
Ireland 298-8 (50 overs): T Tector 73 (81), Campher 66 (50); Smit 4-44

Namibia 168 (41 overs): Green 45 (58), Trumpelmann 40 (34); Moondra 6-26

Ireland win by 130 runs, series tied 2-2

Seamer Jai Moondra finished with the best ever figures for an Ireland bowler in one-day international cricket as the tourists levelled their five-game series against Namibia with a comprehensive 130-run victory.

His 6-26 in Windhoek eclipsed Josh Little's 6-36 against Zimbabwe in 2023, the previous best for Ireland in the format.

With leading all-rounder Mark Adair still to feature in the series despite his place in the touring squad, Ireland's bowlers had allowed their hosts to top 300 twice in the first three games of the series, dropping both to trail 2-1.

But, after Tim Tector marked his ODI debut with a fine knock of 73 off 81 balls to set Namibia a target of 299, this time Moondra put his side in a commanding position with three early wickets to leave the hosts faltering at 32-3.

While a 57-run partnership for the eighth wicket between Zane Green and Ruben Trumpelmann offered brief resistance, Moondra accounted for both in the space of nine deliveries to claim his first international five-wicket haul.

Fittingly, the India-born 29-year-old wrapped up the win with the wicket of Jack Brassell to level the series at 2-2 before Sunday's decider.

Campher continues impressive series with bat

With captain Paul Stirling missing the remainder of the series with a broken finger sustained in the third game, stand-in Lorcan Tucker lost the toss and saw his side put in to bat.

Tim Tector, the younger brother of middle-order batter Harry Tector, took Stirling's place as an opener and had to move through the gears as he adjusted to the unfamiliar format.

Making his ODI debut after eight previous caps in T20 cricket, he reached a maiden half-century in 64 deliveries before accelerating with to a 73 that featured seven fours and three sixes.

Curtis Campher continued to establish himself as Ireland's most consistent player with the bat as he followed Tuesday's century in a losing cause with 66 from 50 balls before falling to a brilliant catch from home captain Gerhard Erasmus.

The all-rounder now has an average of 55 across eight ODIs in 2026, and he found an able partner in George Dockrell who finished on 47 not out.

Moondra's career-best figures then ensured Ireland's batters had done more than enough.

articles.title: South Africa vs Australia: Hosts set up epic finale - what do stats and history suggest could happen?
articles.summary: South Africa set up an epic final day of their decisive Test against Australia by batting throughout the fourth day. What does history suggest could happen?
articles.body:
Third Test, Cape Town (day four of five)

South Africa 329 & 387: Mulder 115, Rickelton 101

A gripping series has the finale it deserves.

Having effectively began day four on 40-4, South Africa batted on and on against Australia in Cape Town to move from a position where defeat looked likely to one where a series victory is a real possibility.

In being bowled out for 387 in the final over - with Ryan Rickelton making 101 and Wiaan Mulder last man out for a brilliant 115 - South Africa set the tourists a target of 288 for victory.

WinViz - the tool analysts CricViz use to predict such results - gives the hosts a 54% chance of victory.

Australia's target is such that should they chase it on day five, it would be the second-highest fourth-innings chase in the 62 previous Tests on this famous ground.

The highest? That's a good omen for Australia.

They chased 331 for a four-wicket win in an epic Test against the Proteas in 2002, when Ricky Ponting hit a brilliant 100 not out.

There have been five other scores above 288 in the fourth innings at Newlands - all of which were made in defeats or when salvaging a draw.

For much of the afternoon and evening sessions, as Australia's bowlers tired, this surface appeared flat enough to score.

When Rickelton and Mulder applied themselves, few opportunities were created. They were able to progress to their third and fourth Test centuries respectively.

It took a run out to end Rickelton's knock, after which Marco Jansen pulled to deep square leg and Gerald Coetzee was also run out - three dismissals down to batter error in a collapse of 4-61, which left South Africa nine down and 251 runs ahead.

That Mulder and number 11 Kagiso Rabada flogged 36 before the close, suggested run-scoring is not impossible.

Pitch turning more but batters more secure

None of those late runs were made under the pressure of a chase, however.

The wicket of Simon Harmer in the final session, bowled shouldering arms by a ball from Nathan Lyon which turned back sharply showed the difficulty ahead.

Harmer dismissed Travis Head, Marnus Labuschagne, Josh Inglis and Alex Carey in Australia's first innings - all recognised batters.

The 37-year-old Essex legend, who once considered playing for England, will be crucial.

As ever in such scenarios, the pitch will play its part.

The PitchViz rating - CricViz's way of assessing the difficulty of a surface - jumped to 6.6 in the final session, comfortably the highest (thus most difficult) rating of the Test.

After settling down in the morning, the ball, as would be expected as a Test progresses, was turning significantly more in the final session than at any point across the previous four days.

Interestingly, however, South Africa's false shot percentage was just 11% across day four, a drop from 18% on day three.

Uneven bounce has not yet been a factor but one ball to Rickelton shortly after tea also shot low.

Intrigue is added by the fact that whoever wins this Test will end the series top of the International Cricket Council's Test rankings.

One man appears to likely to play a huge part in the outcome.

Faced with a target of 205 in the first Ashes Test almost a year ago, Australia opener Head thrashed a sensational 123 from 83 balls to turn a tricky chase into a riotous charge to victory over England.

There was a time, between 2008 and 2019, when Australia had a poor record in situations such as these.

In that period they failed in 14 of their 17 fourth-innings chases when set targets between 200 and 350.

That has changed in recent years, however, with Cummins' men having pulled off pursuits of 282 and 279 since 2023, in addition to the Perth victory last year.

Few sides have been better in key moments in the modern era. Saturday will provide another chance for Australia to deliver under pressure.

articles.title: South Africa vs Australia, third Test: Centuries by Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder lift hosts back into series contention in Newlands decider
articles.summary: Ryan Rickelton and Wiaan Mulder strike centuries as South Africa set Australia 288 to win third Test and seal series victory; series winners take top ‌spot in Test rankings; watch final day live on Sky Sports Cricket from 8am on Saturday
articles.body:
Australia toiled, taking a single wicket in the opening two sessions before a burst after tea, but ​it was still very much the home side's day and sets up ‌an intriguing tussle on Saturday.

Mulder top-scored with 115, his fourth Test century, while Rickelton amassed 101 as the pair ensured Australia ​will need to complete the second-highest successful run chase in 137 years of Test cricket at Newlands.

"It was about trying to win the small moments," Rickelton said. "We knew we ​were effectively 40 for four this morning and that Australia would come hard ⁠at us.

"It was about spending time at the ⁠crease rather than worrying about scoring runs or getting too far ahead of ourselves. We had our plans and needed to stick to them.

"We ‌knew the longer we batted, the more frustrated Australia would become. Perhaps they expected things to happen quite quickly because of the deteriorating wicket."

The pitch is starting to show signs of wear, ‌with Australia batter Josh Inglis saying on Thursday a chase of over 200 would be a difficult one batting last.

They will need considerably more than that at more than three runs an over against a South African bowling attack that has had its feet up for more than a day and a half.

South Africa ⁠resumed on the fourth morning at 140-4 and lost only ​Matthew Breetzke (43) in two sessions as he fell to a pull shot ​off Pat Cummins (2-71) and was caught on the boundary by Mitchell Starc, a familiar mode of dismissal for the home ​side this Test.

Rickelton and Mulder put on 154 for the sixth wicket as they took ⁠few risks and accumulated runs.

There was considerable turn for spinner Nathan Lyon (2-101) and variable bounce for the seamers.

Mulder was the last man out as he tried to up the tempo, caught on the boundary - again by Starc off Cummins - to ⁠bring a close to the day.

The series is level ​at 1-1 after Australia won the first Test by 214 runs in Durban and South ​Africa responded with a victory by an innings and 31 runs in Gqeberha.

"It's been a special series. ⁠It's ebbed and flowed across all three games," ​Rickelton added. "Both teams have got ahead at different stages, only for the ​other to fight back. There have been mistakes and some really good cricket as well.

"Hopefully it comes down to a really ‌good day for South Africa ​tomorrow."

The winners of the match will occupy the No 1 spot in the ‌Test world rankings, which is currently ​held by Australia.

articles.title: ‘I did everything I could for India’: Punam Raut on retirement and her unfinished comeback dream | Interview
articles.summary: Punam Raut spent four years trying to get back into the Indian team.
articles.body: Punam Raut spent four years trying to get back into the Indian team. She scored runs in domestic cricket, recovered from illness and worked towards a comeback. But the call never came.Her last international appearance was in 2021. When Raut announced her retirement earlier this month, it was not because she had stopped wanting to play for India. It was because she had begun to realise that the return she had been working towards might not happen.“I always had the desire to return to the Indian team,” Raut tells TimesofIndia.com. “Unfortunately, that didn't happen.”Raut represented India for more than 12 years, scoring 2,299 runs in 73 ODIs. Her career included an 86 against England in the 2017 Women's World Cup final and a world-record 320-run opening partnership with Deepti Sharma against Ireland that year.India lost the World Cup final at Lord's by nine runs, but the campaign helped change how women's cricket was viewed in the country. For Raut, the memories go beyond the runs. She remembers messages from young girls whose parents had begun encouraging them to play cricket after watching India.Her own journey began when women's cricket offered few guarantees of a career. Her father needed financial help from his employer to buy her first cricket kit. Now, having stepped away from international cricket, Raut wants to concentrate on coaching and mentoring the next generation.In an exclusive conversation with this website, she speaks about the comeback that never materialised, the people who supported her and the innings that helped inspire a generation.Excerpts:After playing international cricket for more than 12 years, your last appearance for India came in 2021. What happened over the last four years that eventually led to your retirement?My only aim over these four years was to make a comeback. I had two very good domestic seasons, finished among the leading run-scorers and performed well in multi-day cricket. But I couldn't get selected, and that's fine.The selectors are focusing on youngsters, and I felt it was becoming difficult to continue at this stage of my career. Since childhood, my dream was to represent India. I lived that dream and achieved my goal. I did everything I could for the country, although I always wanted to return to the team.Before last year's domestic season, I suffered from dengue, followed by pneumonia. I had a lot of joint pain and struggled to recover. I worked hard to regain my fitness, but I realised my body wasn't recovering the way it used to. That also contributed to my decision.I have been mentoring young cricketers for four years. Many were 10-12 when I started working with them; today, they are 14-15 and approaching the competitive level. I felt that if I continued playing for another two or three years, I might not be able to give them the time they need at this crucial stage.It was a very difficult decision. When you've played cricket for so long, retiring is never easy.Your 86-run knock in the 2017 Women's World Cup final against England remains one of the most memorable innings of your career. India fell agonisingly short of the target. What does that innings mean to you today?I am very grateful that I could contribute when India needed it the most. The result didn't go our way, but I feel we gave everything we had. That's how sport is sometimes.I also scored a hundred against Australia and contributed against Pakistan. I was among India's leading run-scorers in that World Cup. Whatever I had to give, I gave everything in that tournament.At that time, there wasn't much money in women's cricket, and not many people watched it. But the way we played changed the perspective of a lot of people.The night before the final, I couldn't sleep, so I opened Facebook and Instagram and started reading the messages I had received. There were messages from young girls and senior citizens. I became very emotional.A lot of girls told me they were able to play cricket because of us. Some said their fathers had encouraged them to take up the sport after watching our performances. Imagine parents who had earlier refused to let their daughters play cricket now encouraging them to pursue it.Some girls even told me they wanted to cut their hair like Punam Di!There were elderly people who had sent their blessings and prayers as well. Reading those messages made me realise that we had genuinely brought about a change.You made your India debut at a time when women's cricket did not enjoy the recognition it receives today. How difficult was it to pursue that dream, especially when it came to convincing your parents and getting the necessary support?It was very difficult. My parents supported me at a time when cricket was barely considered a career option for girls.Despite that, they never doubted me or asked me to reconsider. I told them I loved the game so much that I could play the entire day without getting tired of it.The very next day, my father took me to buy a cricket kit and enrolled me in coaching. His financial situation wasn't particularly strong. During the 2017 World Cup, he told me that his boss had helped him financially when he needed money for my kit and coaching.You won't believe how much that kit meant to me. The moment I got it, my excitement doubled. Everything I had watched on television suddenly became real.I used that kit carefully for around five years because I knew how special it was. The bat, pads and helmet meant so much to me because they represented the beginning of my journey.My parents also faced criticism from people around them, but they continued supporting me. They believed in me, and that played a huge role in helping me reach the Indian team.Indian women's cricket has made significant progress, with the team winning the 2025 World Cup. Having seen the game evolve over the years, where do you think Indian women's cricket still needs to improve to achieve sustained dominance at the global level?We have the talent to dominate women's cricket, and I am confident the day will come when we consistently dominate teams such as Australia, South Africa and England.One major reason for my confidence is the support the BCCI is providing. The girls are getting more matches and opportunities than ever before. Earlier, we would play one or two international series in a year and then go straight into a World Cup. That is no longer the case. The team now plays throughout the year and gets more exposure against different opponents.The Women's Premier League has also made a tremendous difference. Many players who have represented India have benefited from the platform it provides.The pathway from domestic cricket to the international level has improved, too. Players get opportunities through the WPL, India A matches and age-group tournaments. The Under-19 Women's World Cup and state-level premier leagues are creating more opportunities for young cricketers.You have shared the dressing room with Harmanpreet Kaur and Smriti Mandhana, both of whom have led teams successfully. What do you make of their leadership, and how do you see Smriti's experience as captain shaping India's future?Harmanpreet has done a tremendous job as captain. She led India to the Women's World Cup title, which is a historic achievement, and deserves a lot of credit.Smriti has also shown what she can do as a leader. She captained Royal Challengers Bengaluru to the WPL title, which was a significant achievement.I believe Smriti can do very well for India. She has the confidence to lead, and I have always felt that she tends to bat even better when she has the responsibility of captaincy. She has the experience, ability and temperament to take the team forward.In 2017, you and Deepti Sharma put together a record 320-run opening partnership against Ireland. Deepti was still a young player, while you had considerably more experience. How did that partnership develop, and when did you realise you were creating history?Deepti opened with me for the first time because Smriti was injured. We were playing a quadrangular series, and Smriti was undergoing rehabilitation ahead of the World Cup.We were both focused on preparing well for the World Cup. We wanted to give India a good start, and that was our priority throughout the innings.That series was special for me because I had made a comeback to international cricket. I had been dropped in 2016 and spent around eight to 10 months away from the team. During that period, I played domestic cricket and scored plenty of runs.When I returned, I wanted to make the most of the opportunity and contribute to the team's success. Deepti, despite being younger, responded very positively. She was a good partner to bat with.You have now retired from international cricket but continue to work with young cricketers. What are your plans for the future? Would you like to focus entirely on coaching and mentoring, or are you open to other roles in cricket?For now, I am focusing on what is in my hands. I am enjoying my work with youngsters and want to continue doing that.There will be opportunities in the future, whether in commentary, selection, administration, coaching or mentoring. I am open to exploring them, but at the moment, I am happy with what I am doing.Working with young players gives you time to develop them properly. You can work on their technical skills, tactical understanding and mindset. When you see them improving and eventually achieving success, the satisfaction is incredible.What would you like to tell young cricketers who dream of playing for India or making it to the WPL but expect success to come quickly?Success doesn't come overnight. You have to spend time working towards it, sometimes for years, before you begin to see results.Many youngsters tell me they want to play state cricket next year or make it to the WPL as quickly as possible. But that's not how sport works. You need to be patient and understand that development takes time.If you want to pursue cricket or any other sport professionally, you have to be disciplined and committed. Don't look for shortcuts. Don't run after success. Be patient, believe in yourself and keep working hard.One message for your fans?I am extremely grateful to all my fans and well-wishers. When I announced my retirement, I received so many messages, and I was genuinely overwhelmed by the love and support.I am also thankful to the media for acknowledging my performances and recognising my contribution to Indian cricket. I feel fortunate to have such a wonderful fan following.I will continue to stay connected with my fans through Instagram and other social media platforms. I hope to share my experiences, connect with people and add value in whatever way I can.Please continue to love and support me like this. I am truly grateful to all of you.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Chasing big totals is good for cricket': Sanath Jayasuriya
articles.summary: MUMBAI: Sri Lankan batting great Sanath Jayasuriya has given a thumbs-up to the recent trend of teams chasing down big totals on flat pitches in
articles.body: MUMBAI: Sri Lankan batting great Sanath Jayasuriya has given a thumbs-up to the recent trend of teams chasing down big totals on flat pitches in white-ball cricket.Sri Lanka pulled off the second-highest successful chase in ODIs when they overhauled England's 429-run total in a Tri-Series match in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, on October 22."It's very good to see that it's happening and players are getting runs on the board and chasing it, which is good for cricket. Teams and players are getting more and more confident, and that is the key. Anything is possible these days, and it is good to see that teams are putting runs on the board and even chasing, but I can see that is also putting the bowlers under pressure," Jayasuriya told reporters at an event on Friday."It's been a lot of changes in the rules. New things have come up in cricket with new regulations, which are good for the game," he added.Asked about the supremely talented and explosive Abhishek Sharma, who smashed a 38-ball 113, including a 35-ball century, to help India win the third T20I at Wellington by six wickets, Jayasuriya said, "He has a long way to go, but it is a good future for India. Let him play his natural game and let him do his work, and it will be a good investment for Indian cricket.""He (Abhishek) is an all-round player. You cannot say anything in specific is strong — he is an all-round player. He can play in any part of the park, so that is a good thing," he added.Praising India's white-ball team, Jayasuriya said, "They are talented cricketers and are playing well. India has got the talent and is playing good cricket at the moment. There are quite a few Indian players who have been doing well. Good to see them. They are talented, work hard and are playing well."Asked about Sri Lanka's impressive performance in Pakistan in the Tri-Series — they won two of their four matches and qualified for the final, where they will face Pakistan on Saturday — Jayasuriya felt that the campaign would boost their confidence ahead of their white-ball tour of India in December."It's a good confidence (booster) for the Sri Lankan team, which is doing well before they come to India. The confidence is high, they are playing well, and I hope they will do well in India too," the former dashing left-hander, who also served as Sri Lanka's chief selector, said.Jayasuriya backed India to do well in the forthcoming ODI and Test series in New Zealand."They are going to do well for sure, but away from India they have always looked to do well, and it will be a good series," he said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘Fell short with the ball’: Shreyas Iyer reflects on India's defeat, praises Glenn Phillips
articles.summary: Shreyas Iyer admitted India fell short with the ball in the fourth T20I against New Zealand, while praising Glenn Phillips for his match-winning century
articles.body: Shreyas Iyer admitted India fell short with the ball in the fourth T20I against New Zealand, while praising Glenn Phillips for his match-winning century in Auckland on Friday.India suffered an 87-run defeat after New Zealand piled up 259/7, powered by Phillips' 107 off 49 balls and Michael Bracewell's 65 off 25. The hosts then bowled India out for 172/9 to register their first win of the five-match series, making it 3-1.Reflecting on India's bowling performance, Iyer said: "I think we fell a bit short in our bowling to start with. Powerplay, especially in the third over, they got that momentum from there on."The India captain, however, was full of praise for Phillips, who struck six fours and 10 sixes in a stunning knock."Exceptional knock by Glenn. Some phenomenal shots, which were like pure bliss. So kudos to him. He's been consistent throughout the series, so lot to learn from him," Iyer said.India will look to regroup ahead of the final T20I in Hamilton. Iyer said the team would review its performance and work on executing its plans better."I feel that it's important to retrospect, see where we can actually bounce back, coming into Hamilton. So I personally feel that we can probably go back to the drawing board and see to it we analyse and try to execute to the best of our abilities in the next game," he said.Iyer also acknowledged that adapting to the ground dimensions had been a challenge for some players, particularly those experiencing such conditions for the first time."Some of them, it's their first time playing on such grounds. So it takes a bit of time for them to adapt to the challenge. It's not that easy, I understand that," he said.However, he backed the team to learn from the experience, pointing to their performances in the first three matches."The way they executed the first three games, it was magnificent, and yeah, this is just a learning curve. I feel that next time when they come here, they would probably have a better idea on how to go about their business. So a great learning curve, and hopefully we come back positive in the next game," Iyer added.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Auqib Nabi added to India squad for first three ODIs against New Zealand
articles.summary: India have added fast bowler Auqib Nabi to their squad for the first three ODIs against New Zealand, bringing him into the group earlier than initially
articles.body: India have added fast bowler Auqib Nabi to their squad for the first three ODIs against New Zealand, bringing him into the group earlier than initially planned.The right-arm pacer was originally named in the squad for the fourth and fifth matches of the five-game series but will now be available from the opening ODI, starting November 4.The change comes after Prasidh Krishna was ruled out of the entire ODI series due to a hamstring injury sustained during the recent home series against the West Indies. His selection for the New Zealand tour had been subject to fitness clearance.Prasidh, however, remains in contention for the two-Test series against New Zealand. The pacer could be added to the India A squad for the third and final four-day match against New Zealand A, beginning November 7, if he clears his fitness assessment.Pace all-rounder Nitish Kumar Reddy will continue to be part of the ODI squad for the first match before linking up with India A for the third four-day game in Lincoln. The move is aimed at providing him with match practice ahead of the two-Test series, which begins on November 19.India’s updated ODI squad for the first three ODIs: Shubman Gill [C], Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli, Shreyas Iyer [VC], KL Rahul [WK], Axar Patel, Naman Dhir, Anshul Kamboj, Gurnoor Brar, Ruturaj Gaikwad, Arshdeep Singh, Ishan Kishan [WK], Mohammed Siraj, Kuldeep Yadav, Nitish Kumar Reddy (only for the first ODI), Auqib Nabi.
